title: Lincoln Murphy, Sixteen Ventures, Customer Success: Defined
text:
## The Definition of Customer Success
Lincoln Murphy defines Customer Success as: "When our customer achieves their Desired Outcome through their Relationship with us, leading them to stay longer, buy more, and advocate for us." This is an operating philosophy, not merely a belief system, and it is a real business function.

## Customer Success Management (the operating model)
Customer Success Management encompasses the People, Processes, Workflows, Data, and Systems used to move the customer toward their ever-evolving Desired Outcome within the relationship context.

## The Desired Outcome Framework
The formula is Goal plus Appropriate Experience (AX). Earlier iterations phrased this as Required Outcome plus AX. Desired Outcome is the single most important concept: it is what the customer needs to achieve (the Goal) and how they need to achieve it (the Appropriate Experience).

## Goal = Objective + Conditions + Time Frame
A Goal consists of an Objective, Conditions, and a Time Frame. Murphy stresses that "Without a timeframe, a goal is just a wish." Conditions are the specific qualities of the Goal that are essential to the feeling of success: if these are not met, even though the Goal was achieved, the customer will still feel unsuccessful. Example: a CRM customer wants a 250k dollar sales increase by Q4 but needs those customers to average 12k ARR; without that condition met, they would feel unsuccessful.

## Appropriate Experience (AX)
The Appropriate Experience is primarily the Interaction Content, Channels, and Cadence that a customer segment requires to feel successful. Key insight: there is no such thing as a high-touch or a tech-touch customer; there are only customers for whom certain experiences are appropriate.

## Relationship = Interactions + Context
A Relationship is Interactions plus Context. Context is all of the data that we can use to determine whether a customer is on the path toward success, including progress milestones, activity, usage, changes, goals, and contract status. Account ownership is defined as maintaining Context.

## Progress Milestones
A Progress Milestone (previously called a Success Milestone) is an action or event marking a significant change or stage in the customer's journey toward their ever-evolving Desired Outcome. Four flavors: Functional, Operational, Tactical, and Strategic.

## Orchestration and the path to over 100 percent NRR
Orchestration means properly managing expectations with customers that certain things are going to happen in the future, and ensuring that when they do, they are not just expected but anticipated. Murphy calls this arguably the single most important thing for achieving above 100 percent Net Revenue Retention.

## Joint Accountability
Joint Accountability is the shared obligation or willingness to accept responsibility for each party's actions leading to an outcome. Four components: what customers do independently outside the product, what customers do independently inside the product, what the vendor does with customers and their users, and what the vendor does behind the scenes.

## The Success Gap
The Success Gap is the gap that exists between your customer functionally completing the tasks necessary in your product to be successful from your point of view as the vendor, and them actually achieving their Desired Outcome. Closing this gap, not just driving product usage, is the job of Customer Success.

## Coverage Model
The Coverage Model is how your Resources are Organized, Operationalized, and Mobilized to deliver your Customer's Desired Outcome. Resources include team, playbooks, tasks, automation, communication, and the technology stack.

title: Lincoln Murphy, Sixteen Ventures, Customer Onboarding
text:
## The Core Philosophy of Onboarding
Proper onboarding is not done to prevent churn; it is done to ensure the customer achieves their Desired Outcome. There is a critical distinction between vendor success (conversion, the customer paying you) and customer success (the customer achieving their goals). Focus on the latter and the former follows.

## What It Means to Be Onboarded
A customer reaches onboarding completion at one of two states. The first is First Value Delivered (FVD): the customer has achieved initial success with the product. The second is Recognized Value Potential: the customer sees genuine value possibility beyond the sales and marketing messaging. Onboarding is not complete when the customer has finished a setup checklist; it is complete when they have reached first value or clearly see the path to it.

## The Success Milestones Framework
Rather than generic timeline-based communication (Day 1, Day 5, Day 7), map the customer journey backward from the desired outcome. Identify the definition of initial success by asking customers directly. Work backward to identify the required milestones. Trigger communications based on milestone achievement, not calendar dates. Focus lifecycle messaging on the next milestone only, which makes communication more targeted and effective throughout the entire customer lifetime.

## Discovery Questions That Are Not Feature-Focused
Ask what the customer's Desired Outcome is, how they measure success, how they are evaluated by their leadership, and what they are trying to achieve. Avoid asking what features or workflows they need: that yields iterations on existing processes rather than breakthrough solutions and anchors onboarding to your product rather than their outcome.

## Concrete Results
One case study showed average free trial conversion time reduced from 42 days to 3 days using this milestone-driven approach, with a 33 percent increase in Average Subscription Value. Getting the customer to value faster both accelerates conversion and increases the value of the relationship.

title: Dave Kellogg (via ChurnZero), Quick Insights on Customer Success and SaaS Metrics
text:
## Logo Retention vs Dollar Retention
Dave Kellogg prefers ARR-based churn (dollars renewed divided by dollars up for renewal) over logo churn because it captures partial churn where the logo stays but the customer consumes less. Logo churn misses this because the numerator is only logos. A company can retain 95 percent of its logos while losing 15 percent of its dollars if its remaining accounts contract.

## Gross Revenue Retention (GRR)
GRR is a dollar-based revenue retention metric that includes all forms of shrinkage, including shrinkage to zero. Contractions must be included; excluding them undermines the metric's utility. GRR can never exceed 100 percent because it does not count expansion.

## Net Revenue Retention (NRR)
NRR operates as a cohort-based measure where only two snapshots matter: entry valuation and exit valuation. The flows in between do not matter, only the two snapshots do. Reactivations count as expansions within cohorts and are treated as saves.

## Available-to-Renew (ATR) Churn
For customers with early-out clauses, Kellogg recommends ignoring early-outs in ATR calculations and building historical reserves instead. Auto-renew customers count as ATR because they retain a choice; the metric measures, of those who had an option, the percentage who renewed. With mixed auto-renew and finite-term bases, track two separate metrics: overall renewal percentage and renewal percentage among those with an actual choice.

## CSM Compensation
He recommends compensating CSMs roughly 80 percent on NRR targets and 20 percent on CSAT, framing the job as: get the renewal and have the customer expand at the standard rate. For difficult account books forecasted at 75 percent retention, use a sales accelerator comp where OTE is based on hitting 80 percent and leverage increases above that.

## Time to Value as a Threshold, Not an Optimization Target
Time to value is critical, but as a threshold rather than something to over-optimize. Ensuring customers get value within some time T is necessary but not sufficient for renewal. Focus on implementation completion and immediate CSAT.

## CAC and Financial Metrics
For Customer Acquisition Cost, just lag sales and marketing spend by a quarter rather than computing the true sales-cycle lag, which enables cross-company comparability. Startups should not obsess over calculating CLV initially; with one-year deals it is perfect in your first year by definition. Separate subscription COGS (tech ops, cloud hosting, support) from professional services COGS.

## Pay-as-You-Go Impact
Usage-based pricing blows up ATR churn because everyone is ATR all the time, eliminating the metric's utility. The paradigm shifts from who likes you and will renew toward financial modeling of future usage patterns.

## Measuring CSM Performance
Activity metrics are unreliable proxies for value. Prefer CSAT and NPS surveys that ask about CSM effectiveness and relationship quality, and run regression analysis correlating renewal to attributes such as the company cares about my success and the company has great CSMs.

title: SaaS Capital, GRRumbling About Retention Metrics: Pitfalls in Measuring SaaS Churn
text:
## Core Definitions
Net Revenue Retention (NRR) is the sum of period-2 revenue from period-1 customers divided by period-1 total revenue, and it includes upsells and expansion. Gross Revenue Retention (GRR) caps each customer's period-2 revenue at their period-1 level, excluding expansion, so GRR is always less than or equal to NRR. The critical principle: you must use per-customer data to compare periods, and only sum the customers after you have compared periods.

## Anti-Pattern: Aggregating Before Comparing
Using company totals before per-customer comparison covers up losses from some customers with gains from others, obscuring true retention health. This is the single most common retention-measurement error.

## Anti-Pattern: Annual vs Monthly Periods
Annualizing obscures volatility. In one example a company showing 87.5 percent annual GRR masked a Q4 collapse to 50 percent GRR when examined monthly. Compounding monthly retention is extremely sensitive to which two months you use; a single perfect month yields a misleading 100 percent annualized figure, and one customer loss can create a 35 percent distortion. The recommendation is to compare month-over-year-ago-month with 3-month, 6-month, and 12-month trailing averages.

## Revenue Composition Pitfalls
Usage-based pricing creates 1 to 8 percent lower GRR (depending on the variable percentage) because of inherent volatility. Setup and implementation fees should be excluded from ARR: including a 10k implementation on a 90k subscription creates an artificial 90 percent GRR instead of 100 percent. Consider excluding paid trials under 6 months and treating them as one-time revenue. Amortize refunds and credits retroactively rather than booking a lump-sum charge in a later month.

## What Not to Include in Recurring Revenue
Hardware sales, pass-through revenue, custom development, and transactional revenue that varies more than 10 percent month to month should remain outside recurring revenue calculations.

## Discipline Over Gut Feel
Companies that deviate from P&L-recognized revenue (for example segmenting by Ideal Customer Profile or excluding non-regrettable churn) must document this with written, board-approved, objective criteria, never gut feel. Sophisticated investors demand per-customer recalculations, which is why loose cohort-adjusted numbers are unreliable across companies.

title: Bessemer Venture Partners, 10 Laws of Cloud (Law 7: Customer Success is Company Success)
text:
## Law 7: Customer Success is Company Success
Bessemer's canonical framing is that customer success is company success. Enterprise companies should achieve less than 1 percent monthly gross churn, and net expansion (net revenue retention) should exceed 100 percent. A one percent change in monthly renewal rates will result in more than a 100 million dollar difference in your valuation at IPO. Over time, renewals and upsells become the largest drivers of enterprise value: a renewal dollar is cheaper to acquire than new logo ARR because upsell CAC is lower than new-customer CAC. High-performing customer success teams track user adoption, NPS, and engagement as retention leading indicators and align their processes to the customer's executive-level metrics.

## Law 5: The 5 C's of Cloud Finance (Churn)
On churn, the benchmarks are: enterprise logo churn (gross) under 7 percent annually; CARR renewal rates above 100 percent, meaning net negative churn is the goal; and SMB churn around 20 percent gross, which is higher but offset by lower CAC. A rule of thumb is that the CLTV to CAC ratio should be 3x or higher.

## Why Retention Compounds
Because churn compounds against a growing base, small retention improvements produce outsized long-term value. The core operating implication for a CSM organization is to treat renewals and expansion as the primary value engine, and to instrument leading indicators (adoption, engagement, NPS) rather than waiting for the lagging signal of a non-renewal.

title: Gainsight, The DEAR Framework for Customer Health Scoring to Grow and Forecast NRR
text:
## The DEAR Framework for Customer Health
Gainsight's DEAR framework scores customer health across four dimensions: Deployment, Engagement, Adoption, and ROI. It is built to be a leading indicator that forecasts gross and net revenue retention, not a lagging report of what already happened.

## Deployment
Deployment measures customer activation and setup effectiveness by comparing entitlement data (the features a customer has licensed) against activated usage. Poor deployment signals shelfware risk and potential downsell: the customer is paying for capability they never turned on.

## Engagement
Engagement assesses stakeholder involvement and communication cadence. It tracks whether the team is engaging the right people at the right cadence, including contacts with real decision-making influence. It requires identifying key contacts and establishing engagement SLAs, and it distinguishes day-to-day champions from periodic executive check-ins.

## Adoption
Adoption evaluates breadth (the frequency and number of regular users) and depth (usage of sticky features that indicate meaningful, embedded workflows). It relies on telemetry data to measure real product-usage patterns rather than self-reported satisfaction.

## ROI
ROI determines genuine value realization against the customer's identified business outcomes. It uses mutual success plans that document the customer's Desired Outcomes and the verification of a verified outcome being completed. ROI is what separates a customer who uses the product from a customer who is actually succeeding with it.

## Acting on the Score
DEAR connects workflows to leading indicators and lagging outcomes so teams can measure every activity against current and future business impact. CSMs use regression analysis to identify which activities correlate with renewed and expanded customers, and run targeted red-adoption campaigns to convert low-performing scores to green before renewal discussions. Gainsight reports that year after year their actual renewal rates have aligned almost perfectly with DEAR-generated health scores, demonstrating that well-built leading indicators predict retention.

title: Gainsight, The Essential Guide to the Customer Journey and Lifecycle
text:
## Customer Journey vs Customer Lifecycle
The customer lifecycle maps the complete journey a customer takes with your business, from initial discovery to becoming a loyal advocate. The customer journey tracks specific touchpoints; the lifecycle provides the high-level view of relationship stages. A CSM needs both: the stage view to know where the account is, and the touchpoint map to know what to do next.

## The Five Core Stages
Reach (awareness and discovery): the initial brand encounter through search, social, reviews, or word-of-mouth, measured by visitors, impressions, social reach, and brand mentions. Acquisition: converting interest into pipeline through quality-focused lead generation, personalization, self-service, and segmentation, measured by lead conversion rate, cost per lead, and sales-accepted leads. Conversion: the prospect becomes a paying customer, requiring the removal of purchasing friction and clear ROI, measured by conversion rate, opportunity-to-close ratio, and sales cycle length. Retention: sustaining success through onboarding, adoption, support, and proactive engagement, the stage that drives about 61 percent of overall revenue through renewals and expansion in B2B, measured by churn, Net Revenue Retention, health scores, and product adoption. Loyalty: satisfied customers become advocates and referral sources, and returning customers spend 67 percent more than new customers, measured by renewal rates, referral participation, review volume, and advocacy.

## Managing the Lifecycle
Align cross-functional teams across marketing, sales, product, and success. Balance automation with human-first engagement. Track both leading indicators (adoption, sentiment) and lagging indicators (churn, NRR). Establish clear ownership via RACI charts. When mapping the lifecycle, define success criteria per stage, the critical touchpoints and handoffs, team responsibilities, and stage gates with required actions.

## The Economics
Acquiring a new customer costs roughly 5 to 7 times more than retaining an existing one, which is why lifecycle optimization, not just acquisition, is critical for sustainable revenue growth.

title: Gainsight, The Essential Guide to Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs)
text:
## What a QBR Is and Is Not
A QBR is a strategic meeting held quarterly between a vendor and customer, designed to demonstrate ROI, align on shared goals, and deepen the partnership. It is not a status update or a technical troubleshooting session. An EBR (Executive Business Review) typically involves senior leadership, occurs annually or biannually, and takes a strategic long-term view aligning high-level business objectives. QBRs are tactical, frequent, and relationship-focused; EBRs are strategic, infrequent, and executive-aligned.

## Why They Matter
B2B customers who have strong executive engagement are 2.5 times more likely to renew (McKinsey). QBRs strengthen the partnership, demonstrate tangible ROI, create transparency that reduces renewal uncertainty, and build trust through accountability.

## Recommended QBR Agenda
Executive summary (high-level overview), key performance metrics (adoption rates, time-to-value), ROI analysis (concrete business impact), progress against previous goals (celebrate wins, address blockers), benchmarking data (competitive context), customer health update (health score snapshot), and action items and next steps with clear accountability.

## Best Practices
Prepare a focused agenda and distribute it beforehand. Connect data back to the customer's original purchase rationale. Personalize the content to their specific goals and recent milestones. Involve the right stakeholders, both day-to-day users and executives. Set measurable objectives for the next quarter. Update health scores and share insights across the team. Close by scheduling the next QBR and confirming responsibilities.

## Common Mistakes
Do not dwell excessively on negative feedback; focus on solutions. Do not become defensive about criticism. Do not let the meeting exceed roughly 60 minutes. Do not use generic templated content without personalization. Do not end without a scheduled follow-up and clear next steps. Segment accounts (strategic, growth, emerging or at-risk) and adjust the QBR format accordingly rather than running one identical format for every account.

title: Gainsight, How to Run an Executive Business Review That Drives Impact
text:
## Purpose of the EBR
An Executive Business Review is a strategic meeting between company leadership and customer executives focused on business outcomes, value delivery, and future opportunities. It is distinct from the operational QBR, which tracks usage metrics and tactical progress. EBRs are annual or bi-annual with C-suite attendees; QBRs are quarterly with manager-level attendees.

## A Sample EBR Agenda
Welcome and objectives (5 minutes), strategic business updates (10 minutes), outcomes achieved (15 minutes), challenges and opportunities (10 minutes), recommendations and next steps (15 minutes). The largest blocks are the outcomes achieved and the forward-looking recommendations, because the EBR is about value and the future, not a feature demo.

## Preparation
Start 3 to 4 weeks early. Review account plans, conduct stakeholder surveys, and run brief interviews to surface executive priorities. Meet the champion ahead of the review to align on the agenda. Focus quantifiable value on ROI or cost savings realized, operational efficiency improvements, progress toward customer-defined strategic goals, and benchmark comparisons.

## Best Practices and Pitfalls
Discuss challenges transparently (adoption limitations, organizational changes, process gaps) to build trust. Provide forward-looking recommendations on unlocking additional value and roadmap alignment. Avoid these pitfalls: insufficient preparation, treating it as a status update rather than a strategic conversation, using technical jargon instead of business language, overloading with content (focus on 3 to 5 key themes), and neglecting post-review follow-up.

## Cadence by Segment
Strategic accounts get a bi-annual EBR (every 6 months), growth accounts annual, and new customers get their first EBR 3 to 6 months post-implementation.

title: Lincoln Murphy, Sixteen Ventures, Beyond Touch Levels: Scaling CS through Appropriate Experience (AX)
text:
## The Core Premise
There is no such thing as a tech-touch or a high-touch customer. There are only customers and their Appropriate Experience (AX). Touch-level labels reflect internal resource-allocation models, not customer reality. Segmenting by touch level bakes an internal constraint into how you treat customers.

## Anti-Pattern: Revenue-Based Segmentation
Segmenting customers by revenue or ARR fails in three ways. First, it ignores individual context: categorizing by payment alone dismisses each customer's unique journey and engagement needs, and high-revenue customers may thrive with minimal support while low-revenue ones may need intensive engagement. Second, it creates entitlement and churn: assuming high-paying customers deserve more engagement regardless of actual need breeds dissatisfaction. Third, it misallocates resources: a revenue focus either overwhelms CSMs managing many low-touch accounts or underutilizes those handling a few high-touch clients who do not need constant contact.

## The AX-Driven Approach
Appropriate Experience operates on three principles. It is individual-centric: understand each customer's journey, needs, and preferences through active listening. It is holistic: it encompasses the pre-purchase experience, the product experience, and all post-sale touchpoints. It is dynamic and data-driven: customer needs evolve, so you continuously refine the experience using feedback.

## Scaling Through AX
AX enables real capacity planning by matching engagement intensity to actual customer needs rather than revenue tier, by identifying Good Fit customers with the willingness and ability to receive the required support, and by allocating resources proactively rather than reacting to overload. Segment by shared Appropriate Experience, not by how much the customer pays.

title: Jason Lemkin, SaaStr, CLTV Isn't The Whole Story: Second-Order Revenue
text:
## What Second-Order Revenue Is
Second-order revenue is the revenue generated beyond the initial customer sale. It comes from champion job changes, when a key contact moves to another company and brings your product with them (roughly a 10 percent occurrence rate); from word-of-mouth and referrals, existing champions recommending you to peers (roughly a 30 percent conversion rate); from expansion within existing customers through upsells and cross-sells over time; and from viral effects and natural advocacy.

## Why First-Order CLTV Understates Value
Standard first-order-only CLTV analyses underestimate the true revenue generated by customers by 50 to 100 percent in most SaaS models. All-in CLTV that includes second-order revenue is approximately 2x higher than the typical calculation. If you only count the direct dollars a customer pays you, you systematically undervalue your best customers and under-invest in keeping them happy.

## A Concrete Example
Take a baseline enterprise customer paying 10,000 dollars in Year 1, expanding 25 percent to 12,500 in Year 2, and 25 percent again to 15,625 in Year 3, for direct revenue of about 38,125 over three years. Adding second-order effects, where champions refer others and later re-buy elsewhere, raises the all-in figure to roughly 60,000.

## Strategic Implication
Because second-order effects compound and generate revenue with minimal additional acquisition cost, organizations should optimize Sales, Marketing, and Customer Success as one cohesive investment rather than treating them as separate budgets. Customer Success is not a cost center: it is the engine of the largest and cheapest revenue you will ever generate.

title: Bain and Company, Net Promoter System, Measuring Your Net Promoter Score
text:
## The Ultimate Question
The Net Promoter Score is built on one question: How likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague, scored on a 0 to 10 scale.

## The Three Categories
Promoters score 9 to 10: they are loyal, enthusiastic customers who drive referrals (more than 80 percent of referrals) and increase their purchases. Passives score 7 to 8: they are satisfied but vulnerable, with repurchase and referral rates about 50 percent lower than promoters, and they are susceptible to competitor switching. Detractors score 0 to 6: they are unhappy customers who generate more than 80 percent of negative word-of-mouth and churn at high rates with reputational damage.

## The Calculation
Net Promoter Score equals the percentage of Promoters minus the percentage of Detractors. Passives count toward the total number of respondents but are not added or subtracted, so they pull the score toward zero.

## Score vs System
There is an important distinction: NPS is the specific metric, and the Net Promoter System is the broader operating framework for building a customer-centric organization using that metric, including closing the loop with customers who respond. A score with no follow-up action is a vanity number; the system is where the value is.

## Why It Matters
Sustained value creators have Net Promoter Scores two times higher than the average company, and NPS leaders grow at more than twice competitor rates. The metric can be tracked across business units, products, service teams, segments, geographies, and functional groups, not just at the company level.

title: Dave Kellogg, Kellblog, Should Customer Success Report into the CRO or the CEO?
text:
## The Question
Kellogg argues that in early and mid-stage SaaS companies, Customer Success should report to the CEO, not the CRO.

## The Leaky Bucket
Sales pours new ARR into the bucket; Customer Success prevents it from leaking out. As a company scales, the renewal bucket dwarfs the new-customer bucket because of subscription economics, so the CS leader eventually commands a larger ARR pool than the new-sales leader.

## The Incentive Problem Under a Single CRO
When both Sales and CS report to a single CRO who is essentially the VP of New Sales, perverse incentives emerge: Sales may book deals they know probably will not renew, and CS loses its role as the organizational check and balance. Kellogg's line: the only thing worse than dealing with the problems caused by this check and balance is not hearing about those problems.

## Hunters and Farmers
Hunters do new customer acquisition and non-incidental expansion (cross-sells to new buyers). Farmers do renewals and incidental expansion (upsells, seat additions). Separating the reporting lines lets each specialize without one function cannibalizing the other.

## Five Arguments for CS Reporting to the CEO
It keeps Sales focused exclusively on winning deals rather than account management; it preserves the organizational tension that prevents inception churn (bad-fit deals); it enables cross-functional collaboration without a hierarchy conflict; it creates a career pathway (SDR to CS to Sales) for skill development; and it orients CS toward revenue-generating activities rather than being treated as a support function.

title: Dave Kellogg, Kellblog, The Three Types of Customer Success Manager
text:
## Why Three Types Matters
Kellogg argues that Customer Success Manager is not one job but three, and conflating them causes hiring and compensation mistakes. Mapping duties to person-type matters: assign renewal responsibilities to a product-focused CSM and you get poor results; assign pure adoption work to a sales-oriented CSM and they lack intrinsic motivation for it.

## The Product-Oriented CSM
Focus: product expertise, implementation, technical guidance, and proactive health checks. Philosophy: ensure you get the best use of our products. Background: often from consulting or technical roles. Their natural conversations center on feature adoption and technical problem-solving.

## The Process-Oriented CSM
Focus: renewal management, satisfaction monitoring, adoption tracking, and escalation coordination. Philosophy: manage systematic touchpoints and organizational relationships. Background: typically project management. Their natural conversations address renewal timelines, stakeholder changes, and training events.

## The Sales-Oriented CSM
Focus: account expansion, upsell opportunities, renewal ownership, and cross-divisional growth. Philosophy: ensure the customer gets maximum benefit from, and makes maximum use of, our software. Background: often promoted from sales development. Their natural conversations pursue expansion opportunities and stakeholder introductions.

## The Practical Lesson
Sales-oriented CSMs naturally own renewals and pursue expansion, while product-oriented CSMs resist renewal responsibility organizationally. Decide which type your business model needs before you write the job description and the comp plan, rather than hiring one type and expecting the behavior of another.

title: Dave Kellogg, Kellblog, Stopping Inception Churn: The Prospective Customer Success Review
text:
## What Inception Churn Is
Inception churn is churn that is effectively built in from inception: the customer was sold a solution the system was never designed to deliver, so they embark on a doomed implementation with a low or zero probability of success from day one. This is the anti-pattern that no amount of great post-sale CSM work can fix, because the deal was un-successable when it was signed.

## The Core Problem
Sales pursues deals despite warnings from presales, consulting, and professional-services teams who recognize fundamental misalignment. Multi-year contracts delay accountability beyond typical executive tenure, which lets bad-fit deals close because nobody will be around when they fail.

## The Damage
Direct costs include lost CAC recovery (a 100-unit customer churning after year one, at a 1.5x CAC ratio and 75 percent margins, produces a 75-unit net loss) and PS burnout (failed implementations can consume 150 to 225 units trying to rescue a 100-unit deal). There is also market reputation destruction in tight early-stage communities via analysts, social, and review sites, plus demoralization across PS and CS. Metrics deteriorate: elevated churn, reduced expansion, and diminished lifetime value that threaten future financing.

## The Solution: Prospective Customer Success Review Committee (PCSRC)
A cross-functional committee with senior representatives from sales, presales, professional services, customer success, and finance. The mechanism is an Andon Cord flagging system that lets anyone escalate a high-risk deal for review before it closes; typical flaggers are presales or post-sales consultants who spot success-inhibiting constraints. The committee either proposes a lower-risk deal alternative that realigns customer expectations with product capabilities, or it incentivizes abandoning the deal when success probability is negligible. The success metric is not deals rejected at committee, it is inception churn reduced through deals that were never signed.

title: Lincoln Murphy, Sixteen Ventures, SaaS Churn Rate
text:
## Acceptable Churn Benchmarks
Murphy cites the Bessemer Venture Partners standard of 5 to 7 percent annual churn (customer or revenue based). Pacific Crest survey data showed roughly 70 percent of SaaS companies achieved under 10 percent annual churn, and 75 percent of those were at 5 percent or below.

## Monthly vs Annual: The Compounding Trap
A critical distinction: 5 to 7 percent annual churn equals only about 0.42 to 0.58 percent monthly churn. But 5 percent monthly churn compounds to approximately 46 percent annual churn, calculated as 1 minus 0.95 to the 12th power. Reporting a monthly number as if it were an annual number is a common and dangerous error.

## Logo vs Revenue Churn
Murphy distinguishes customer (logo) churn from revenue (dollar) churn, but stresses that high churn undermines growth regardless of which method you use. Revenue churn can be negative (net negative revenue churn) when expansion within the retained base exceeds losses.

## Churn Is a Symptom, Not the Disease
There are two root drivers of churn: customer business failure, which you have limited control over, and customers failing to achieve their Desired Outcome, which is controllable. Churn is just a symptom of an underlying disease and requires a root-cause solution, not symptom treatment. By the time churn shows up in the metric it is a lagging indicator; you prevent it by acting on leading indicators much earlier.

## The Vicious Cycle and Bad-Fit Acquisition
In low-revenue segments, companies often fail to deliver the appropriate customer experience because it is unprofitable to provide, which triggers churn, and then they cut support further, which accelerates departures. Churn is often designed in at acquisition through poor customer fit, made worse by inadequate onboarding and support for low-value cohorts. The fix starts at who you acquire, not at the renewal.

title: Gainsight and Bessemer Venture Partners, The Ten Laws of Customer Success (Laws 1 to 5)
text:
## The Ten Laws Overview
The Ten Laws of Customer Success, sponsored by Bessemer Venture Partners and produced by Gainsight, are the guiding principles for delivering world-class retention. Each law is authored by a recognized CS leader. In the Customer Success movement, companies add a third core process beyond building product and selling product: driving Customer Success. All business questions are reframed around the customer's success.

## Law 1: It's a Top-Down, Company-Wide Commitment (Nick Mehta, Gainsight)
Customer Success is not a department, it is a philosophy that must pervade the entire company. It requires setting the tone from the CEO and board, making difficult decisions that prioritize retention over quarterly sales targets. Reframe every function around success: which feature truly helps clients achieve their goals (product), which clients are a good fit (sales), which messages authentically align with the value delivered (marketing), which metrics reflect real customer success (finance). Establish early-warning metrics such as health score, adoption score, and NPS, and pay for the behavior you want by adding CS metrics (net retention, NPS, health score) to the bonus plan.

## Law 2: Sell to the Right Customer (Ted Purcell, Clarizen)
The wrong customer damages your organization: you incur the CAC, and the bigger cost is the opportunity cost of applying resources to customers who struggle and doubling down as they fail. Marketing must target the right kinds of customers and sales must quickly disqualify those who are not a great fit, going beyond budget and executive-sponsorship qualification. The churn itself is only the tip of the iceberg; the cost of signing customers you cannot make successful can be enormous. Give CS leadership visibility, and consider veto power, over deals that are not a fit.

## Law 3: The Natural Tendency for Customers is Towards Churn (Karen Pisha, Code42)
Customers and vendors start like two boats side by side, but if unoccupied they drift apart; change is the enemy (people change, business models change, leadership changes). In many SaaS companies the lifetime value of a customer is 10 times the value of the initial sale. Partial churn is the loss of contract dollars in a situation where the customer does not fully leave (product churning, unused licenses returned, or a deeper renegotiated discount). Top churn reasons include value not realized, stalled implementation, loss of the project sponsor or power user, low product adoption, acquisition, missing features, new leadership, and poor product quality. Most companies do not catch on until it is too late to save the account; the trick is watching for the warning signs and acting on the data.

## Law 4: Customers Expect You to Make Them Wildly Successful (Nello Franco, Talend)
Customers do not buy features and functions; they buy your solution because they want to achieve a business objective. To make a customer wildly successful you must know three things: how they are measuring success (their unit of currency), whether they are achieving that value or on a realistic path to it, and what their experience is along the way. ROI is not a concept, it is an equation: quantify the expected results. Set an early milestone (Phase 1 Value) to deliver a quick win and keep momentum, then get on a cadence of strategic business reviews. A QBR that only covers product roadmap and open support cases is extremely defensive; there is no way to win if all you talk about is features that do not yet exist.

## Law 5: Relentlessly Monitor and Manage Customer Health (Dan Steinman, Gainsight)
Customer health is to Customer Success what the sales pipeline is to a sales VP: the predictor of future behavior. Read the phrase four ways, emphasizing customer health, then manage, then monitor, then relentlessly. In the perpetual-license world as much as 90 percent of lifetime value is collected at the initial sale, but in subscription the initial deal is worth less than 10 percent of total lifetime value: a 25,000 dollar annual contract over a 7 to 10-plus year life means nine renewals and, even at only 5 percent annual growth, the customer spends well over 10 times the initial deal. Possible health components include product use, customer support, survey scores, marketing engagement, community involvement, contract growth, self-sufficiency, invoice history, and executive relationship. Build a component-based score so an individual CSM can act: if product adoption shows only 13 of 100 licenses active, getting 60 users active moves the score up. Analytics with no action are largely useless; do not just observe and ponder, do something.

title: Gainsight and Bessemer Venture Partners, The Ten Laws of Customer Success (Laws 6 to 10)
text:
## Law 6: You Can No Longer Build Loyalty Through Personal Relationships (Bernie Kassar, Mixpanel)
Businesses scale only when customers scale, which means a long tail of lower-value customers who in aggregate are valuable but individually do not merit white-glove treatment. You must deliver value to the bottom of the segmentation pyramid without much one-to-one interaction, so loyalty comes from the value customers get from the product, not the relationship with an individual. The playbook: segment customers by a metric that fits your business (most B2B by ARR), define a coverage model, create interaction categories, establish a cadence, build a community, and create a feedback loop. Coverage guidance: a high-touch CSM might manage 5 to 15 accounts, a medium-touch CSM 20 to 50; high-touch is reserved for complex accounts with high ARR (say 500,000 dollars or more). Interaction categories: high-touch (in-person meetings, QBRs, a blueprint success plan, executive one-to-ones), medium-touch (a quarterly meeting plus monthly video), and tech-touch (webinar-style one-to-many, monthly to quarterly newsletter, email campaigns).

## Law 7: Product Must Be Priority No. 1 (Kirsten Maas Helvey, Cornerstone OnDemand)
The key to retention, satisfaction, and scaling the support and service org is a well-designed product married to a best-in-class experience. The main root of dissatisfaction is usually the product: the harder it is to use, the harder it is to make the client successful. Use a client-engagement framework that drives community, engagement, and clear feedback loops, including Product Advisory Councils (PACs) led by product management and Communities of Practice (COPs). You cannot manage what you do not measure: CSAT (overall satisfaction, usually a 5-point scale, benchmark against history), NPS (loyalty, not satisfaction, 0 to 10 scale, percent 9 to 10 minus percent 0 to 6), and Customer Effort Score (CES, ease of doing business, 1 to 7 agreement scale).

## Law 8: Obsessively Improve Time to Value (Diane Gordon, Brainshark)
Buyers expect to see value in a reasonable time frame, and for SaaS that frame is the length of the subscription: if the customer has not seen real value by the time renewal discussions begin, they are far less likely to renew. There is a direct correlation between the length of onboarding and the likelihood of the first renewal (if it takes 11 months to go live on a 12-month contract, the odds are poor). The secret: work with the customer to establish concrete success measures, implement iteratively for early value (do not boil the ocean, hit the simplest measure first), and adjust in real time the moment expected value is at risk. Define success measures with the business sponsor while you still have their attention during the sales cycle. To size the prize, multiply 30 days by the number of customers to get the additional selling days you gain by improving time to value by 30 days, or use 5 days as a conservative multiplier.

## Law 9: Deeply Understand the Details of Churn and Retention (Kathleen Lord, Intacct)
Even a 1 percent increase in churn can make a huge difference: at a 25 million dollar run rate trying to hold 50-plus percent growth, a 1 percent churn increase means sales must close an extra 20 percent in new business to maintain the rate. Committed Monthly Recurring Revenue (CMRR) is the combined value of all recognized recurring subscription revenue plus signed contracts going into production, minus churn. Track renewal CMRR in granular buckets: cancellations, downgrades, upgrades, first-time archives. Example: a 50,000 dollar contract renewed at 55,000 breaks down as 45,000 apples-to-apples renewal, 8,000 churn of product B, 14,000 upsell of product A, and 4,000 from a discount moving 25 percent to 22 percent. Unavoidable churn is often called death and marriage (a customer going out of business or getting acquired). Best practice is to complete all renewals 30 to 60 days in advance of the subscription end date, and to model expected CMRR (prior-year renewals 25 million, assumed 10 percent churn 2.5 million, planned expected CMRR 22.5 million). Use an unbiased third party to run post-churn interviews.

## Law 10: Customer Success Teams Must Become Metrics-Driven (Jon Herstein, Box)
Maturity requires repeatability, process definition, measurement, and optimization, echoing the Capability Maturity Model (CMM) levels: Initial, Repeatable, Defined, Managed, Optimizing. At Level 1 (Initial), work gets done through heroics with poorly defined CSM roles, which buys short-term customer happiness but long-term pain (overworked people, inconsistent results). Three categories of metrics: customer and user behavior (NPS, logins, feature usage), CSM activity (frequency of QBRs and touches, support tickets handled by CSMs, timeliness of risk identification, effectiveness of mitigation), and business outcomes (satisfaction, churn, expansion). A caution from Nick Mehta: user behavior is only a proxy for the business value the customer derives, because no one buys your software so they can log into it; understand the customer's actual objectives and jointly agree how you will measure them.

title: Jason Lemkin, SaaStr, What Are The Churn Benchmarks for SaaS?
text:
## Churn and Retention Benchmarks by Segment
Jason Lemkin's core point is that churn must be read by segment, never as a single blended number. Consumer SaaS typically churns at 6 to 7 percent a month, which is why it requires very low customer acquisition cost and minimal sales infrastructure. Very Small Businesses (VSB) commonly churn at 3 to 5 percent a month due to business failures, distraction, and payment issues. Small-to-Medium Businesses (SMBs) should target retaining 95 to 100 percent of their revenue each year, net of upsells and upgrades; HubSpot required years to reach 100 percent net revenue retention in this segment. Enterprise customers should show 110 to 120 percent, or even more, annual expansion through net negative churn, driven by seat additions, tier upgrades, and feature expansion.

## Why the Aggregate Misleads
Blending cohorts across customer sizes produces misleading aggregate metrics, because a healthy enterprise book can hide a bleeding SMB book and vice versa. Churn numbers also shift depending on whether you include or exclude trials, credit-card failures, and win-back customers within 90 days, so a single quoted figure is nearly meaningless without its definition. The right focus is the quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year churn-reduction trajectory rather than an absolute benchmark.

## The Anti-Pattern: Growth Masking Churn
High growth can mask high churn for only so long. Once year-over-year growth slows toward 100 percent, roughly 3 percent monthly churn cuts your growth rate in half, which is why churn must be addressed before it becomes structural. By or well before 10 million dollars in ARR, a healthy company should have material net negative churn.
